paper.title: A computational framework for optimal and Model Predictive Control of stochastic gene regulatory networks
paper.label: Paper
paper.abstract: Engineering biology requires precise control of biomolecular circuits, and Cybergenetics is the field dedicated to achieving this goal. A significant challenge in developing controllers for cellular functions is designing systems that can effectively manage molecular noise. To address this, there has been increasing effort to develop model-based controllers for stochastic biomolecular systems, where a major difficulty lies in accurately solving the chemical master equation. In this work we develop a framework for optimal and Model Predictive Control of stochastic gene regulatory networks with three key advantageous features: high computational efficiency, the capacity to control the overall probability density function enabling the fine-tuning of the cell population to obtain complex shapes and behaviors (including bimodality and other emergent properties), and the capacity to handle high levels of intrinsic molecular noise. Our method exploits an efficient approximation of the Chemical Master Equation using Partial Integro-Differential Equations, which additionally enables the development of an effective adjoint-based optimization. We illustrate the performance of the methods presented through two relevant studies in Synthetic Biology: shaping bimodal cell populations and tracking moving target distributions via inducible gene regulatory circuits.

paper_title: Towards Big Biology:: high-performance verification of large concurrent systems
combination_points: formal verification of large concurrent systems
compositional model checking of interacting processes
temporal-logic specification of safety, liveness, and ordering constraints
runtime verification / closed-loop monitoring of concurrent state transitions
scalable abstraction-reduction methods for high-dimensional biological dynamics
combination_plan: Treat the living-material program as a concurrent system whose modules—protein-material conjugation, metabolite sensing, genetic regulation, and matrix remodeling—are verified as interacting processes with temporal constraints. Use compositional formal verification or runtime monitoring to enforce orthogonality, viability bounds, and spatiotemporal sequencing, enabling a predictive closed-loop controller that detects unsafe crosstalk or deadlocks and reprograms module activity accordingly.
justification: Even without the abstract, the title indicates high-performance verification of large concurrent systems, which provides a transferable abstraction for coordinating many interacting biological control loops. The problem’s core bottleneck is not just building biological parts but ensuring their concurrent, orthogonal, spatiotemporal operation; formal concurrency verification offers mechanisms for specifying, checking, and monitoring such coordinated behavior.

paper_title: Systems and control theoretic approaches to engineer robust biological systems
combination_points: closed-loop feedback control architecture for biological systems
robustness and stability analysis under biological uncertainty
predictive or model-based control for dynamic regulation
orthogonal control channels and modular system decomposition
sensing-actuation loops linking intracellular state to extracellular outputs
combination_plan: Use systems-and-control theory to formalize the living-material platform as a multi-input/multi-output closed-loop system, where molecular interfacing, metabolite sensing, genetic regulation, and matrix remodeling are modeled as coupled subsystems with feedback, feedforward, and predictive controllers. Robust control and stability criteria can then be used to coordinate spatiotemporal interventions while preserving viability and orthogonality across control channels.
justification: The candidate paper’s focus on systems and control theoretic engineering of robust biological systems provides a direct transferable abstraction for the original problem’s central bottleneck: creating a unified, predictive, closed-loop programming framework across molecular, cellular, and extracellular processes.
